qid: Who is the individual implicated by allegations in articles from Fortune, The Verge, and TechCrunch, suggesting he built a successful crypto exchange on falsehoods, used a proxy for unauthorized access to customer funds, struggled with managing rapid company growth, and is accused of committing fraud for personal gain?

# SEC alleges FTX was fraudulent enterprise built on Bankman-Fried's customer fund theft

The Verge reported on 2023-10-10 that the Securities and Exchange Commission alleges FTX was a fraud "from the start," with the defining characteristic being a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange, faces seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. Caroline Ellison, former head of Alameda Research (FTX's sister hedge fund), testified that Bankman-Fried directed her to commit crimes including fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering. She stated: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back." Ellison pleaded guilty to criminal charges related to the scheme.


---


# Prosecutor Rehn's framing of Bankman-Fried as fraud built on deception

Fortune reported on 2023-10-04 that prosecutor Thane Rehn opened the government's case against Bankman-Fried by arguing his success "all of it, was built on lies" because "behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn's roughly 30-minute opening statement contrasted Bankman-Fried's public persona—a successful FTX CEO assuring customers their money was safe—with the alleged reality: he secretly diverted customer funds through Alameda Research to finance his lifestyle, political donations, and risky investments. The warrant for this fraud claim centers on the gap between his public assurances of safety and his undisclosed use of customer money, concealment from employees, and forged financial documents to lenders and investors.


---


# Bankman-Fried accused of spending billions in stolen FTX deposits on personal real estate, investments, and Alameda repayment

The Verge reported on 2023-09-28 that Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is accused of misusing customer funds. According to the indictment, Bankman-Fried used "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" for three purposes: purchasing over $200 million in real estate for himself, making billions of dollars in personal investments, and repaying Alameda Research's lenders. The indictment details how special code features created at Bankman-Fried's direction permitted Alameda unlimited withdrawals from FTX while he publicly denied such privileged access existed.


---

The Verge reported on 2023-09-28 that prosecutors allege Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, used "more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions." Notably, prosecutors may introduce evidence of these contributions during trial "even though they aren't part of the charges brought" against Bankman-Fried, who faces seven counts including wire fraud and conspiracy charges related to misappropriation of FTX customer deposits.

# OpenAI to position GPT store as dominant AI distribution platform in 2024

TechCrunch predicted on 2023-12-19 that OpenAI will aggressively promote the GPT store as the primary distribution channel for AI tools throughout 2024, following Apple's app-store model. The store, originally scheduled for December 2023 launch but delayed due to leadership upheaval, will be "pushed hard as the platform to get your AI toys and tools from, and never mind Hugging Face or any open source models." This hypothesis assumes the store successfully ships and becomes a major distribution channel; it is falsified if the store fails to launch or remains marginal. qid: Has the description of ChatGPT's capabilities by TechCrunch remained consistent between the article published on September 28 and the subsequent article on November 30?

The distinction reflects that ChatGPT represented a change in how existing capability—built on GPT-3.5—reaches ordinary people, rather than a research advance in model capability itself. Biderman noted that "previously you needed to have some skill, albeit not be an expert, to consistently get usable stuff out of [text-generating models]. ---


# ChatGPT lowered the skill threshold for usable text-generation output, making it the central object of AI research and development

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-30 that ChatGPT's primary impact has been redirecting the AI field's attention toward itself rather than representing a fundamental algorithmic breakthrough. Stella Biderman, an AI researcher at Booz Allen Hamilton and EleutherAI, stated that "the primary impact [ChatGPT] has had [is] encouraging people training AIs to try to mimic it, or encouraging people studying AIs to use it as their central object of study." Biderman explained that previously, "you needed to have some skill, albeit not be an expert, to consistently get usable stuff out of [text-generating models]." This placement itself constitutes the scarce asset that Google and competitors vie for, as evidenced by Google's $26.3 billion spend in 2021 to secure default status across platforms including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. Pichai justified this spending by asserting that defaults drive query volume, which yields data that improves search quality, which in turn justifies further default payments. According to The Verge's account of his testimony, Pichai stated that "Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices." This cyclical logic—more queries yield better products, better products justify premium placement costs—represents company assertion rather than established fact. By controlling which search engine appears by default on devices and browsers through exclusive agreements, Google prevents rivals from accumulating the query volume and user data necessary to train and refine competitive search products. Pichai stated that Google "pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices." The argument positions Google's payments—roughly $18 billion of which went to Apple alone that year—as a natural consequence of offering a superior product that consumers and partners willingly choose, rather than as anticompetitive behavior designed to block competitors.

Helena World Chronicle argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content through multiple mechanisms: older technologies like the Knowledge Graph (launched May 2012, containing 500 billion facts by 2020) and Featured Snippets, as well as newer AI systems including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella stated he was willing to spend $15 billion annually to secure Bing as Apple's default search engine, while DuckDuckGo's CEO testified their search engines "would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple." Google that Apple never seriously considered switching to another search provider or building its own search product during the 2016 renegotiation of the Information Services Agreement with Google CEO Sundar Pichai. # Cue's conflicting testimony on Apple's Google Search deal

The Verge reported on 2023-09-26 that during US v. Google antitrust proceedings, Apple executive Eddy Cue presented two simultaneous claims that created tension throughout his testimony. Cue stated that "Apple believes in protecting its users' privacy, and it also believes in Google," yet the court explored whether these positions could coexist. 

The Justice Department pressed Cue on whether Apple selected Google as the default search engine on all Apple devices because it was the superior product or the most lucrative deal. Cue argued "there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" and maintained Apple chose Google "because we've always thought it was the best." However, opposing counsel then presented evidence of Apple's internal criticism of Google's privacy practices, making the compatibility of Apple's stated privacy commitment and its Google partnership the day's central question.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article claim that Google's anticompetitive behavior specifically harms news publishers' revenue, while The Age article suggests a general acceptance of foul play by Google without specifying the impact on revenue?

# Google accused of starving publishers by redistributing content and costing billions in lost revenue

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court in D.C. by Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle asserts Google engages in anticompetitive behavior harming news publishers. The complaint argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on its own platforms, causing publishers to lose "billions of dollars" in revenue. The suit specifically cites Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as exacerbating the problem, alongside older technologies like the Knowledge Graph launched in May 2012 and Featured Snippets that redirect user traffic away from publishers' websites.

# Google AdSense rate changes cited as anticompetitive harm to publishers in antitrust suit

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action antitrust complaint filed by Helena World Chronicle against Google and Alphabet includes allegations that Google's modifications to AdSense rates have caused economic harm to news publishers. The lawsuit characterizes these rate changes as "evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part" and positions them alongside other practices as anticompetitive conduct within the digital news advertising market. The complaint argues such changes exemplify Google's broader pattern of siphoning publisher revenue through unlawful means, situating AdSense rate modifications within the larger antitrust violation framework alleging that Google "starves the free press."


---


# Helena World Chronicle files Sherman Act class action against Google and Alphabet over content siphoning

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based news publisher, filed a class action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for D.C. accusing Google and parent company Alphabet of violating antitrust law, specifically the Sherman Act and other federal antitrust statutes. The complaint alleges that Google engages in anticompetitive conduct by using technology to "siphon off" publishers' content, readers, and advertising revenue. Helena World Chronicle argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content through multiple mechanisms: older technologies like the Knowledge Graph (launched May 2012, containing 500 billion facts by 2020) and Featured Snippets, as well as newer AI systems including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard. The suit contends that SGE answers 75% of user queries without requiring clicks to publisher websites, and that publishers cannot block SGE because it uses GoogleBot, Google's general search crawler. The complaint seeks damages, an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent before using their data for AI training, and a requirement that publishers opting out of SGE remain visible in search results.


---


# Google rejects Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit as meritless

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that Google disputed the class action antitrust lawsuit filed by Arkansas-based Helena World Chronicle. TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action antitrust lawsuit filed by Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle contends Google uses its Search Generative Experience (SGE) anticompetitively. According to the suit, SGE operates through a conversational search interface that answers user queries without requiring click-throughs to publisher sites, reducing traffic. Publishers cannot block SGE because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot. Fortune reported on 2023-10-04 that during opening statements in the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, the prosecution characterized Caroline Ellison, CEO of Alameda Research and Bankman-Fried's "on-again off-again girlfriend," as a front concealing his scheme. Prosecutor Thane Rehn alleged that using Ellison, Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money at FTX. The defence countered by blaming Ellison herself, arguing she "did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets." By trial date, Ellison had become a government cooperator, though the source notes she was not among the initial witnesses called—described as "former lieutenants-turned-government-cooperators."

The Verge reported on 2023-10-10 that the Securities and Exchange Commission alleges FTX was a fraud "from the start," with the defining characteristic being a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange, faces seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. Caroline Ellison, former head of Alameda Research (FTX's sister hedge fund), testified that Bankman-Fried directed her to commit crimes including fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering. She stated: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back." Ellison pleaded guilty to criminal charges related to the scheme.

# Prosecutor Rehn's framing of Bankman-Fried as fraud built on deception

Fortune reported on 2023-10-04 that prosecutor Thane Rehn opened the government's case against Bankman-Fried by arguing his success "all of it, was built on lies" because "behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn's roughly 30-minute opening statement contrasted Bankman-Fried's public persona—a successful FTX CEO assuring customers their money was safe—with the alleged reality: he secretly diverted customer funds through Alameda Research to finance his lifestyle, political donations, and risky investments. The warrant for this fraud claim centers on the gap between his public assurances of safety and his undisclosed use of customer money, concealment from employees, and forged financial documents to lenders and investors.

The Verge reported on 2023-10-10 that Caroline Ellison's case exemplifies a uniquely damaging form of romantic betrayal rooted in inverted accountability. The author argues Ellison was appointed named co-CEO of Alameda Research, the "sin-eater hedge fund," while being "refused" equity—a reversal that makes her the "paradigmatically terrible ex-boyfriend case." This framing rests on how Bankman-Fried weaponized corporate structure against personal trust: he "directed" Ellison to commit crimes including fraud and money laundering while maintaining plausible deniability through her titular authority. # Google's reinforcing-cycle justification for default-placement spending

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in the U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spent in 2021 to secure default search engine placement across platforms. Pichai justified this spending by asserting that defaults drive query volume, which yields data that improves search quality, which in turn justifies further default payments. According to The Verge's account of his testimony, Pichai stated that "Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices." This cyclical logic—more queries yield better products, better products justify premium placement costs—represents company assertion rather than established fact. TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Google CEO Sundar Pichai defended the company's search engine placement deals during U.S. antitrust litigation by arguing the company is simply engaging in lawful business competition. TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google centers on deals making Google the default search engine across devices and browsers. This placement itself constitutes the scarce asset that Google and competitors vie for, as evidenced by Google's $26.3 billion spend in 2021 to secure default status across platforms including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based news publisher, filed a class action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for D.C. accusing Google and parent company Alphabet of violating antitrust law, specifically the Sherman Act and other federal antitrust statutes. The complaint alleges that Google engages in anticompetitive conduct by using technology to "siphon off" publishers' content, readers, and advertising revenue. Helena World Chronicle argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content through multiple mechanisms: older technologies like the Knowledge Graph (launched May 2012, containing 500 billion facts by 2020) and Featured Snippets, as well as newer AI systems including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard. The suit contends that SGE answers 75% of user queries without requiring clicks to publisher websites, and that publishers cannot block SGE because it uses GoogleBot, Google's general search crawler. The complaint seeks damages, an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent before using their data for AI training, and a requirement that publishers opting out of SGE remain visible in search results.

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-13 that Google confronted three distinct antitrust matters concurrently as of mid-November 2023. The Department of Justice's landmark trial against Google was ongoing, the company had "last week settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group," and "on November 6, Google went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games." The Epic Games trial focused on "whether Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure."


---


# Helena World Chronicle lawsuit alleges Google destroyed evidence via chat message spoliation, citing Epic Games precedent

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that the class action antitrust lawsuit filed by Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle against Google includes allegations of improper evidence destruction. The suit claims Google engaged in "spoliation of evidence" through "destruction of chat messages"—an issue previously raised in Epic Games' antitrust case against Google over app store practices, which Epic won. The Helena World Chronicle complaint points to this established precedent to support its contention that Google has systematically destroyed evidence relevant to anticompetitive conduct claims.


---


# Antitrust actions surrounding Helena World Chronicle's December 2023 Google lawsuit

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that the Helena World Chronicle antitrust filing occurred amid multiple concurrent Google legal challenges. The U.S. DOJ pursued a digital ad technology monopoly suit against Google. Separately, a 2020 DOJ civil suit targeted Google's search and search-advertising practices under the Sherman Act. Epic Games filed an app-store antitrust case against Google, which Epic won. Internationally, Google reached a settlement with Canada in November 2023, agreeing to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) annually for news content use, "with funds distributed based on the news outlets' headcount," establishing a precedent for publisher compensation that informed the Helena World Chronicle complaint's demands for consent-based AI training data usage.


---


# Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 as basis for Epic's Google antitrust claims

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games planned to invoke U.S. antitrust law against Google in trial beginning that day. The Sherman Act provides two statutory grounds for Epic's case: Section 1 addresses "restraints of competition," while Section 2 addresses "monopolization." Epic alleged Google engaged in anticompetitive behavior regarding its Android app store, Google Play, and commission structure. Epic would argue that Google restrains competition in two markets: distribution of apps to Android users and payment processing for Android app content.


---


# Epic's antitrust case against Google traced to September 2019 discovery email, culminating in December 2023 verdict

The Verge reported on 2023-12-12 that Epic Games' four-year legal battle against Google originated in a September 2019 email discovered during litigation. Tim Sweeney, Epic's CEO and controlling shareholder, described the sequence: the email outlined "a plan to draw Google into a legal battle over antitrust," followed by a four-week trial concluding with a federal jury verdict on December 11, 2023. The jury found Google maintained an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. Sweeney stated the outcome marked "a great day for all developers," representing the first major antitrust verdict against a tech company with industry-wide consequences since "the US v. Microsoft" in the 1990s. The discovery email functioned as the documented origin point for the entire proceeding.


---


# Google rejects Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit as meritless

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that Google disputed the class action antitrust lawsuit filed by Arkansas-based Helena World Chronicle. A Google spokesperson characterized the suit, which alleges anticompetitive behavior regarding news content and AI training, as "meritless," rejecting both the complaint's antitrust allegations and its claims about harm from AI technologies like Search Generative Experience and Bard.


---


# Index of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 US v Google trial coverage

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-13 a roundup of developments in the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google. The article covers case significance and potential remedies; concurrent Google antitrust matters including the Epic Games trial (begun November 6) and Match Group settlement; declassified revenue-ranked search queries from September 22, 2018, "a list of popular search terms ordered by revenue"; vertical search dominance in categories like car insurance and flights; mechanics of Google's mobile app distribution agreements (MADAs) and revenue-share agreements (RSAs) with manufacturers, per testimony from Google Android employee Jamie Rosenberg on November 8; and Expedia's grievances regarding Google's ad practices, stating "Expedia has a bone to pick with Google."


---


# Epic v. Google trial (Nov 6, 2023): claims, markets, defenses, and key agreements

TechCrunch reported on November 6, 2023 that Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google centered on alleged anticompetitive behavior in Google Play and app commission structure. Epic brought claims under Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2, California's Cartwright Act, and Unfair Competition Law, alleging Google restrains competition in "the distribution of apps to Android users and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps."

Google's defense included User Choice Billing—reducing commissions by 4% for developers using third-party payment processors—and citing competition from Samsung Galaxy Store and Amazon Appstore. Epic challenged Anti-Fragmentation Agreements (AFAs) preventing OEM modification of Android and highlighted "Project Hug," arguing Google paid competitors to avoid distributing outside Play Store. The case examined deals with OnePlus and Samsung, examining whether Google's developer agreements were anticompetitive.


---


# State antitrust laws Epic will invoke against Google in Oakland trial

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games planned to bring antitrust claims against Google under California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law alongside federal Sherman Act violations. Epic stated it would "bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act, and the Unfair Competition Law." The case centers on Google Play's app distribution practices and commission structure for Android devices.


---


# Google AdSense rate changes cited as anticompetitive harm to publishers in antitrust suit

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action antitrust complaint filed by Helena World Chronicle against Google and Alphabet includes allegations that Google's modifications to AdSense rates have caused economic harm to news publishers. The lawsuit characterizes these rate changes as "evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part" and positions them alongside other practices as anticompetitive conduct within the digital news advertising market. The complaint argues such changes exemplify Google's broader pattern of siphoning publisher revenue through unlawful means, situating AdSense rate modifications within the larger antitrust violation framework alleging that Google "starves the free press."


---


# Epic's two-market antitrust theory against Google's Android ecosystem

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games filed an antitrust lawsuit against Google alleging anticompetitive behavior in Android. Epic frames its case around two separate markets: "the distribution of apps to Android users and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps." The company argues Google restrains competition through exclusive billing requirements, anti-fragmentation agreements with device manufacturers that restrict sideloading, and selective developer incentives. Epic contends 90% of apps download through Google Play despite alternatives like Samsung's Galaxy Store existing, and cites Google's bundling of Play Store with other Google services as anticompetitive leverage.


---


# Google antitrust ruling hypothesized to affect parallel Big Tech cases

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-13 that the US v Google antitrust judgment may create precedent affecting separate enforcement actions against competing technology firms. The publication states: "The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases." Specifically, the source identifies three parallel matters potentially influenced by Judge Amit Mehta's ruling: the FTC's September 2023 lawsuit against Amazon for anticompetitive monopoly maintenance; the DOJ's multi-year investigation into Apple's third-party app policies; and the ongoing FTC case against Facebook, in which the agency seeks divestiture of Instagram and WhatsApp. This hypothesis remains falsifiable if those cases proceed to judgment or settlement without material modification based on Google precedent.

# Default search engine placement as scarce asset in Google antitrust litigation

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google centers on deals making Google the default search engine across devices and browsers. A default search engine is the query service preselected by a device or browser maker so users search through it without setup action. This placement itself constitutes the scarce asset that Google and competitors vie for, as evidenced by Google's $26.3 billion spend in 2021 to secure default status across platforms including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. Internal Google data from 2007 showed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they performed "15% more Google searches," establishing early recognition that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share."


---


# Google's defense: dominance through superior product, not illegal conduct

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Google CEO Sundar Pichai defended the company's search engine placement deals during U.S. antitrust litigation by arguing the company is simply engaging in lawful business competition. Google contends that partners like Apple choose it as the default search engine because "it's the best," and that this market dominance does not constitute illegal conduct despite the company spending $26.3 billion in 2021 to secure default positions across platforms. Pichai stated that Google "pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices." The argument positions Google's payments—roughly $18 billion of which went to Apple alone that year—as a natural consequence of offering a superior product that consumers and partners willingly choose, rather than as anticompetitive behavior designed to block competitors.

qid: Between the report from The Verge on the Epic v. Google case and the subsequent report from TechCrunch on the same case, was there disagreement on the nature of Epic Games' arguments against Google?
context:
# Epic v. Google trial delayed 1,180 days while Apple case reached decision in 2021

The Apple case went to trial in 2021 and reached a ruling that September "mostly decided in Apple's favor," with both parties awaiting potential Supreme Court review. By contrast, the Google lawsuit faced repeated delays before finally reaching trial on November 6th, 2023—"a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued." Epic claimed Google operates an illegal monopoly in Android app distribution and payment processing, while Google argued the relevant market included competition from Apple's iPhone ecosystem.


---


# Epic's anticompetitive agreement theory: OnePlus and Samsung examples

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games' antitrust case against Google relies on claims that Google uses anticompetitive agreements with device manufacturers to entrench Google Play's dominance. Epic cites two specific episodes as evidence.

First, Epic references its agreement with OnePlus to distribute Epic Games through the Epic Games app on OnePlus devices, which "OnePlus had to cancel the deal over concerns that the arrangement would have it bypassing the Google Play Store." This cancellation allegedly demonstrates Google's ability to prevent manufacturers from offering alternative app distribution channels.

Second, Epic highlights a deal between Google and Samsung, arguing that Google designed the agreement "to prevent the Galaxy Store from being a competitive threat and require Google Play Billing on apps distributed by Samsung." Epic frames this arrangement as Google leveraging its market power to suppress Samsung's competing app store and force Google's payment system onto third-party developers distributing through Samsung's platform.

Together, these cases form Epic's argument that Google uses manufacturer agreements as exclusionary tools rather than competitive accommodations.


---


# Epic's antitrust case against Google traced to September 2019 discovery email, culminating in December 2023 verdict

The Verge reported on 2023-12-12 that Epic Games' four-year legal battle against Google originated in a September 2019 email discovered during litigation. Tim Sweeney, Epic's CEO and controlling shareholder, described the sequence: the email outlined "a plan to draw Google into a legal battle over antitrust," followed by a four-week trial concluding with a federal jury verdict on December 11, 2023. The jury found Google maintained an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. Sweeney stated the outcome marked "a great day for all developers," representing the first major antitrust verdict against a tech company with industry-wide consequences since "the US v. Microsoft" in the 1990s. The discovery email functioned as the documented origin point for the entire proceeding.


---


# Epic's Sherman Act argument against Google: anticompetitive agreements despite sideloading legality

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games filed antitrust claims against Google under Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act and California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. Epic's core argument targets what it characterizes as "anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers." Unlike its Apple lawsuit, Epic cannot argue that no alternative app installation method exists, since Android permits sideloading. However, Epic contends that "the bulk of its arguments will center around what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers," asserting that Google's contractual arrangements with original equipment manufacturers and app developers restrain competition in app distribution and payment processing markets, regardless of sideloading's technical availability. Epic specifically challenges Anti-Fragmentation Agreements preventing device makers from modifying Android and developer programs like Project Hug that Epic claims discourage apps from distributing outside Google Play.


---


# Helena World Chronicle lawsuit alleges Google destroyed evidence via chat message spoliation, citing Epic Games precedent

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that the class action antitrust lawsuit filed by Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle against Google includes allegations of improper evidence destruction. The suit claims Google engaged in "spoliation of evidence" through "destruction of chat messages"—an issue previously raised in Epic Games' antitrust case against Google over app store practices, which Epic won. The Helena World Chronicle complaint points to this established precedent to support its contention that Google has systematically destroyed evidence relevant to anticompetitive conduct claims.


---


# Epic v. Google trial begins after 1,180-day delay

The Verge reported on 2023-11-05 that Epic Games' antitrust lawsuit against Google proceeded to trial on November 6th, 2023, "a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued." This contrasts sharply with Epic's parallel case against Apple, which reached trial in 2021. Epic alleges Google operates an illegal monopoly in Android app distribution and in-app payment processing, requiring developers to pay the "Google tax" through mandatory fees on its app store.


---


# Epic's antitrust model relies on Microsoft OS monopoly precedent

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games' antitrust case against Google draws its legal theory from prior Microsoft rulings. Epic will argue that Google abuses a monopoly position in Android app distribution similarly to how Microsoft was found to have abused its operating system monopoly. In the Microsoft case, "courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and were abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices." Epic plans to apply this precedent to Google Play, arguing Google makes sideloading and alternative app stores cumbersome for Android users, though Epic cannot claim Android entirely blocks alternatives as it did against Apple.


---


# Android sideloading undercuts Epic's monopoly argument against Google

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games' antitrust case against Google differs from its Apple lawsuit because "this time, Epic can't allege there's no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple, because Android does allow for sideloading apps." Unlike Apple's closed ecosystem, Android permits users to install applications from sources outside Google Play. Epic will instead argue that Google makes sideloading cumbersome and will focus its case on allegedly anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers, rather than claiming an absolute absence of alternative distribution channels.


---


# Epic concedes Google avoided explicit no-compete contracts in opening arguments

The Verge reported on 2023-11-07 that during opening statements in Epic v. Google, Epic's lead attorney Gary Bornstein acknowledged Google "was too clever" to draw up contracts that specifically forced developers not to compete with the Play Store. Bornstein's admission undercuts Epic's no-compete allegation by revealing the absence of written terms explicitly prohibiting competition. Instead, Epic's case rests on alleged conduct—such as payments to developers like the "$360 million" to Activision—rather than contractual language barring rivals from building competing app stores or launchers.


---


# Epic v. Google trial structure: opening statements complete, evidentiary phase begins

The Verge reported on 2023-11-07 that following opening arguments in early November 2023, the Epic Games v. Google trial entered its evidentiary phase to test competing claims about Android's market structure and Google's conduct. Epic's lead attorney Gary Bornstein asserted that "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," citing a $360 million payment allegedly made to Activision. Google's opening countered that its dominance results from legitimate competition with Apple's iOS ecosystem rather than anticompetitive conduct. The court will now examine Epic's core allegations—that Google uses payments and contractual restrictions to prevent competing app stores—against Google's defense that Android's openness, evidenced by preinstalled alternatives like Samsung's Galaxy Store, demonstrates lawful market behavior. The contested meaning of Android's "openness" will be heavily litigated in subsequent trial weeks.


---


# Google displayed Epic's internal messages suggesting awareness of policy violations during trial opening

The Verge reported on 2023-11-07 that during Epic Games v. Google trial opening arguments, Google presented Epic's internal communications to suggest Epic knew it was violating company policy. The messages included "How do we not look like the bad guys?" and "everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" Google used these out-of-context statements to paint Epic as the aggressor rather than Google itself, contrasting with Epic's strategy of portraying Google as a monopolistic bully blocking app store competition on Android.

qid: Do the articles from Sporting News discussing sportsbooks' practices indicate that sportsbooks consistently adjust their odds and lines in response to events and information, such as injuries, roster changes, and gathered data on NBA rookies, or do they suggest different practices for these adjustments?

# Betting lines move with public action and new information

Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that posted betting lines and odds are not static fixtures. "Betting lines and odds are then subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game." Sportsbooks adjust lines or odds when the public bets heavily on one side, and they shift in response to injury reports, roster news, and other developments before game time. This dynamic means the same bet carries different odds across sportsbooks depending on each book's exposure and betting patterns.


---


# Oddsmakers use computer models analyzing analytics, statistics, and matchup data to set sportsbook lines

Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that the best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services to set their lines and odds. These professionals use "computer models and algorithms that consider analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, matchup data, and more to develop the lines and odds." The generated opening lines and odds then remain subject to adjustment based on betting public reaction and new information before games. Other sportsbooks typically copy the lines established by these oddsmakers rather than developing independent models.


---


# Sportsbooks price identical bets differently due to independent liability management and timing

Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that betting lines and odds differ across sportsbooks because "the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook. While one sportsbook may be forced to move a line or change the odds because of betting, another won't."

Each sportsbook manages its own betting liability independently. When the public bets heavily on one side of a wager, a sportsbook adjusts its line or odds to balance exposure and protect profit. Because sportsbooks experience different betting volumes and patterns from their customer bases, they react at different times and to different degrees. Additionally, "the lines and odds may even be different right from the jump," meaning initial prices diverge before any public betting occurs. These compounding factors—distinct liability positions, asynchronous public reactions, and varying opening prices—create persistent pricing gaps for the same bet across competing sportsbooks, making line shopping a rational strategy to secure better odds or more favorable spreads.


---


# Sports betting apps use two distinct pricing models: some set odds independently, others copy established lines

Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that the sports betting industry uses two different approaches to odds-setting. "The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services to set their lines and odds. Other sports betting apps simply copy those lines." Oddsmakers and services that set original lines use computer models and algorithms incorporating analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data. Apps that copy rather than generate their own lines rely on the prices established by these primary oddsmakers, creating a two-tier system where some sportsbooks are price-setters and others are price-takers.

Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that sportsbooks operate on a model designed to balance risk across outcomes. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," the outlet explained. By achieving balanced action, sportsbooks capture the profit margin already embedded in their odds and lines—known as the vig—independent of which side wins. This model means sportsbooks move lines and adjust odds in response to public betting patterns to maintain equilibrium rather than to predict game outcomes.

Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that futures betting requires line shopping because odds fluctuate more than standard game lines. This dynamic means the same bet carries different odds across sportsbooks depending on each book's exposure and betting patterns.

# Sportsbook profit model: evening betting action to capture the vig

Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that sportsbooks operate on a model designed to balance risk across outcomes. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," the outlet explained. By achieving balanced action, sportsbooks capture the profit margin already embedded in their odds and lines—known as the vig—independent of which side wins. This model means sportsbooks move lines and adjust odds in response to public betting patterns to maintain equilibrium rather than to predict game outcomes.


---


# Sports betting apps use two distinct pricing models: some set odds independently, others copy established lines

Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that the sports betting industry uses two different approaches to odds-setting. "The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services to set their lines and odds. Other sports betting apps simply copy those lines." Oddsmakers and services that set original lines use computer models and algorithms incorporating analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data. Apps that copy rather than generate their own lines rely on the prices established by these primary oddsmakers, creating a two-tier system where some sportsbooks are price-setters and others are price-takers.

Online sportsbooks post odds on NBA Rookie of the Year candidates, and bets are settled at season's end. Bettors access these markets through the futures tab on sportsbook websites after creating an account and making a deposit.

Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that betting lines and odds differ across sportsbooks because "the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook. While one sportsbook may be forced to move a line or change the odds because of betting, another won't."

Each sportsbook manages its own betting liability independently. When the public bets heavily on one side of a wager, a sportsbook adjusts its line or odds to balance exposure and protect profit. Because sportsbooks experience different betting volumes and patterns from their customer bases, they react at different times and to different degrees. Additionally, "the lines and odds may even be different right from the jump," meaning initial prices diverge before any public betting occurs. These compounding factors—distinct liability positions, asynchronous public reactions, and varying opening prices—create persistent pricing gaps for the same bet across competing sportsbooks, making line shopping a rational strategy to secure better odds or more favorable spreads.

Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that line shopping—comparing odds and lines across multiple sportsbooks—applies to "any bet," including moneylines, point spreads, totals, and prop bets. Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that line shopping is "the process is as simple as checking the lines and odds for your prospective bet at multiple online sports betting sites." Line shopping works because sportsbooks do not post identical odds and lines—differences emerge immediately or develop as betting volume shifts public money toward one side. These variations allow bettors to reduce their stake or increase potential winnings by selecting the best-priced option across competing sportsbooks.

Sporting News reported on 2023-11-06 that once a wager is placed and locked in at a sportsbook, the original bet cannot be repriced if the line subsequently moves in the bettor's favor. The only recourse when odds improve is to "place additional action at the improved odds or more favourable line." This means a bettor who locked in a line before it shifted cannot retroactively apply the better terms to their existing wager—they must place a separate new bet to capitalize on the movement.

Sporting News reported on 2023-10-04 that the NBA Rookie of the Year award functions as "part of NBA futures betting," allowing bettors to wager on which player will win the honour. qid: Does 'The Verge' article suggest that Sam Bankman-Fried's inability to manage FTX and Alameda Research was due to the companies' growth, while 'Fortune' focuses on his successful persuasion of Adam Yedidia to join his ventures, and 'TechCrunch' alleges that Sam Bankman-Fried committed fraud for personal gain, indicating different aspects of his leadership and actions?

Fortune reported on 2023-10-04 that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, opened with prosecutors and defence presenting fundamentally opposing characterizations. qid: Did the report from The Verge on Apple's defense of its Google Search deal published on September 25, 2023, and the TechCrunch article detailing what was learned about the Google antitrust case involving Apple published on October 31, 2023, show a consistency in the portrayal of Apple's actions regarding its choice of search engine and browser options for iPhone users?
context:
# Google–Apple search deal: mutual obligations blocking competition since 2003

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that under a Google–Apple agreement dating to 2003, Google pays Apple (approximately $18 billion annually as of 2021) to make Google the default search engine. In exchange, "Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users," according to Bloomberg reporting cited in the article. This restriction prevents Apple from switching to a Google competitor or offering users browser choice during iPhone setup. The deal exemplifies how Google's $26.3 billion spend across all platforms in 2021 to secure default placements functions to block competition: by controlling the default position and restricting promotion of alternative browsers, Google maintains search dominance while Apple receives substantial payments but forgoes competitive alternatives.


---


# Apple maintained Safari and blocked browser choice under Google search deal

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that under its search agreement with Google, "the agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor or allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones." Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users through banners, pop-ups, or other means in Google apps, according to Bloomberg reporting cited in the article. CEO Sundar Pichai admitted Google attempted to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on iOS devices in 2018, but Cook declined. The search deal between Google and Apple has been in place since 2003.


---


# Five trial revelations from Google antitrust case, 30–31 October 2023

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 five evidentiary points from Google CEO Sundar Pichai's testimony in the U.S. government's antitrust case. First, Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms, with approximately $18 billion going to Apple; Pichai testified that "the decision was made with the consumer in mind." Second, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users as part of its Apple deal, preventing the use of "banners, pop-ups and other annoying means." Third, Pichai admitted attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on iOS devices in 2018. Fourth, the DOJ questioned Google's policy of deleting internal chat messages despite litigation holds, with messages automatically deleting every 24 hours unless manually changed. Fifth, a 2007 email shown in court revealed Google's early understanding that homepage defaults drive search volume: "when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches."


---


# Google–Apple default search agreement duration by 2023 trial

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Google had maintained its default search engine deal with Apple since 2003, meaning the agreement spanned roughly two decades by the time of the 2023 antitrust trial. According to the source, "Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003." The $18 billion annual payment from Google to Apple under this arrangement became a focal point in the U.S. Department of Justice's case challenging Google's search market dominance.


---


# Apple received roughly $18 billion of Google's $26.3 billion 2021 default payments

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to be the default search engine across platforms, "about $18 billion of that total amount went directly to Apple," according to a New York Times report published earlier that month. Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified in the antitrust trial on October 28 that the $26.3 billion total covered payments to multiple browsers, phones and platforms from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Google has maintained its search default deal with Apple since 2003.


---


# DOJ's implicit argument: Apple prioritizes ISA payments over stated privacy values in Google default choice

The Verge reported on 2023-09-26 that during US v. Google testimony, the DOJ constructed an implicit economic argument against Apple's "best product" rationale for making Google the default search engine. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw questioned whether Apple selected Google because it was "the most lucrative choice or the best product," establishing the question as "a key part of the DOJ's entire case against Google."

The warrant for this reading comes from Apple's own trial exhibits and testimony. Eddy Cue acknowledged the Information Services Agreement "didn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup" and that Apple "make[s] Google be the default search engine because we've always thought it was the best." Yet Bellshaw then presented "a series of emails and slides in which Cue and Apple railed against Google's privacy policies," highlighting the tension: Apple publicly disparages Google's privacy practices while contractually centering Google on its platform. The DOJ's framing suggests financial incentive, not product merit, explains this contradiction.


---


# The 2020 Google search dominance antitrust claim tried in October 2023

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that the October 2023 trial of Google's antitrust case concerns "a 2020 antitrust claim over Google's dominance in the online search market." This lawsuit is "separate from one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado," which targets Google's alleged anticompetitive practices in digital advertising. The search dominance claim challenges Google's default search engine agreements with partners like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla—deals through which Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to maintain its market position across multiple platforms.


---


# Default search engine placement as scarce asset in Google antitrust litigation

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google centers on deals making Google the default search engine across devices and browsers. A default search engine is the query service preselected by a device or browser maker so users search through it without setup action. This placement itself constitutes the scarce asset that Google and competitors vie for, as evidenced by Google's $26.3 billion spend in 2021 to secure default status across platforms including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. Internal Google data from 2007 showed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they performed "15% more Google searches," establishing early recognition that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share."


---


# Index: Eddy Cue's testimony in US v. Google, 2023-09-26

The Verge reported on 2023-09-26 that Apple executive Eddy Cue testified before Judge Amit Mehta in US v. Google in Washington, DC. Cue defended the Information Services Agreement (ISA), the search-default deal between Apple and Google in place since 2002. He testified about renegotiating the ISA with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016, when Apple sought higher revenue-share percentages; the parties "eventually compromised on some other number" and reached agreement. Cue argued "there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" and declined to consider walking away, saying "it was in Google's best interest, and our best interest, to get a deal done." DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed whether Apple's choice reflected Google's superior product versus economic incentives. She questioned iPhone setup's lack of search-engine choice while Apple offers users choices on appearance, location tracking, and app tracking—highlighting the tension between Apple's privacy positioning and its Google relationship.


---


# Google sought iPhone preinstallation deal with Apple in 2018

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified on October 30, 2023, admitting Google attempted to secure preinstallation of its services on every iOS device. Pichai "admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018." Cook declined the proposal because "Apple doesn't preload third-party software onto its devices, and it wasn't going to make an exception for Google." Pichai framed the arrangement as mutually beneficial: Google would gain search users and data; Apple would increase revenue from the existing search agreement between the companies.


---


# Default search engine definition in iPhone setup context

The Verge reported on 2023-09-26 that in US v. Google testimony, Apple executive Eddy Cue defined a default search engine as the preselected option presented during iPhone setup that users must actively change rather than affirmatively select. Under the Information Services Agreement (ISA) negotiated in 2016, Google is made the default search engine on all Apple devices. Cue testified that "We make Google be the default search engine" and "let users easily change it," acknowledging the ISA "didn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup." Cue argued against offering multiple search engine options during setup, stating "We try to get people up and running as fast as possible."

qid: Which company is facing allegations of anticompetitive behavior in both the app distribution and payment processing markets for Android, as well as being accused by a news publisher of harming their bottom line by siphoning off content, readers, and ad revenue, as reported by TechCrunch?
context:
# Epic's two-market antitrust theory against Google's Android ecosystem

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games filed an antitrust lawsuit against Google alleging anticompetitive behavior in Android. Epic frames its case around two separate markets: "the distribution of apps to Android users and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps." The company argues Google restrains competition through exclusive billing requirements, anti-fragmentation agreements with device manufacturers that restrict sideloading, and selective developer incentives. Epic contends 90% of apps download through Google Play despite alternatives like Samsung's Galaxy Store existing, and cites Google's bundling of Play Store with other Google services as anticompetitive leverage.


---


# Google AdSense rate changes cited as anticompetitive harm to publishers in antitrust suit

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action antitrust complaint filed by Helena World Chronicle against Google and Alphabet includes allegations that Google's modifications to AdSense rates have caused economic harm to news publishers. The lawsuit characterizes these rate changes as "evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part" and positions them alongside other practices as anticompetitive conduct within the digital news advertising market. The complaint argues such changes exemplify Google's broader pattern of siphoning publisher revenue through unlawful means, situating AdSense rate modifications within the larger antitrust violation framework alleging that Google "starves the free press."


---


# Epic v. Google trial (Nov 6, 2023): claims, markets, defenses, and key agreements

TechCrunch reported on November 6, 2023 that Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google centered on alleged anticompetitive behavior in Google Play and app commission structure. Epic brought claims under Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2, California's Cartwright Act, and Unfair Competition Law, alleging Google restrains competition in "the distribution of apps to Android users and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps."

Google's defense included User Choice Billing—reducing commissions by 4% for developers using third-party payment processors—and citing competition from Samsung Galaxy Store and Amazon Appstore. Epic challenged Anti-Fragmentation Agreements (AFAs) preventing OEM modification of Android and highlighted "Project Hug," arguing Google paid competitors to avoid distributing outside Play Store. The case examined deals with OnePlus and Samsung, examining whether Google's developer agreements were anticompetitive.


---


# Market definition determines monopoly liability in antitrust cases

The Verge reported on 2023-11-05 that market definition is "one of the biggest questions the court will decide" in Epic Games' antitrust lawsuit against Google over Android app distribution and payments. Market definition fixes the boundaries of the relevant market: if courts define it narrowly as "Android app distribution," Epic's monopoly allegations gain traction; if broadly as "phones and app stores" generally, Google prevails. The Verge explained that "if the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google's on the road to victory. If it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape." The same conduct—Google's app store fees and payment processing requirements—becomes lawful or unlawful depending on whether the market is drawn to include iPhone competition or exclude it.


---


# Epic's two alleged Google monopoly markets in Android ecosystem

The Verge reported on 2023-11-05 that Epic Games alleges Google holds illegal monopolies in two distinct markets: "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing." Epic argues that anyone buying or developing for Android phones "is stuck paying the Google tax," since Google makes it difficult for developers and users to circumvent its app store and its standard fees. The court must first decide the scope of the relevant market—whether it encompasses all phones and app stores generally, or specifically Android-focused distribution and payment channels—to determine if Google's control constitutes unlawful monopoly power.


---


# Google's Android monopoly ties app distribution to payment control

The Verge reported on 2023-12-12 that a federal jury found Google operates an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store. The jury's two findings form a single structural relation: the app store functions as the monopolised product while the billing system operates as the tied product. This coupling means Google's control over Android distribution converts directly into control over payment processing. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, who attended the trial in person, framed the verdict as validation that "the Sherman Antitrust Act works in the new era of tech monopolies," representing the first major antitrust verdict against a tech company with meaningful consequences since US v. Microsoft in the 1990s.


---


# Index to The Verge's Epic v. Google explainer (Hollister, 2023-11-05)

The Verge reported on 2023-11-05 that Sean Hollister's Epic v. Google explainer structures the trial as organized around several key topics. The August 13th, 2020 trigger events—when Epic deployed a Fortnite hotfix bypassing app store payment fees and both Apple and Google removed the app—provide essential background. The parties present competing legal claims: Epic alleges Google maintains "an illegal monopoly" on Android app distribution and in-app payment processing, while Google argues Apple provides sufficient competition since "people can choose to buy an iPhone instead." Market definition emerges as "one of the biggest questions the court will decide"—whether the relevant market encompasses all phones and app stores or specifically Android ones. The explainer also references the Apple case precedent, noting that trial "resulted in a ruling where Apple (mostly) won" and that the Apple judge "ended up" applying a different market definition entirely.


---


# Google accused of starving publishers by redistributing content and costing billions in lost revenue

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court in D.C. by Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle asserts Google engages in anticompetitive behavior harming news publishers. The complaint argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on its own platforms, causing publishers to lose "billions of dollars" in revenue. The suit specifically cites Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as exacerbating the problem, alongside older technologies like the Knowledge Graph launched in May 2012 and Featured Snippets that redirect user traffic away from publishers' websites.


---


# Epic's monopoly theory links Google Play dominance to higher consumer prices through restricted app-store competition

The Verge reported on 2023-11-07 that Epic Games' case against Google rests on proving Google Play Store operates as an unlawful monopoly that inflates consumer app prices. Epic attorney Gary Bornstein argued that Google "bribes" or "blocks" competitors, resulting in "the vast, vast majority of Android app installs" coming from Google Play rather than alternatives like Samsung's Galaxy Store. Epic's legal filings have suggested that "we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and / or lower app store and payment processing fees." Epic pointed to Google's "fat app profit margins (70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year)" and cited a $360 million payment allegedly made to Activision to prevent it from opening a competing app store. The theory frames Google's market position not as natural competition with Apple iOS, but as anticompetitive conduct that harms consumers through higher prices.


---


# Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 as basis for Epic's Google antitrust claims

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games planned to invoke U.S. antitrust law against Google in trial beginning that day. # Helena World Chronicle files Sherman Act class action against Google and Alphabet over content siphoning

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based news publisher, filed a class action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for D.C. accusing Google and parent company Alphabet of violating antitrust law, specifically the Sherman Act and other federal antitrust statutes. The complaint alleges that Google engages in anticompetitive conduct by using technology to "siphon off" publishers' content, readers, and advertising revenue. Helena World Chronicle argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content through multiple mechanisms: older technologies like the Knowledge Graph (launched May 2012, containing 500 billion facts by 2020) and Featured Snippets, as well as newer AI systems including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard. The suit contends that SGE answers 75% of user queries without requiring clicks to publisher websites, and that publishers cannot block SGE because it uses GoogleBot, Google's general search crawler. The complaint seeks damages, an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent before using their data for AI training, and a requirement that publishers opting out of SGE remain visible in search results.

Epic Games filed an app-store antitrust case against Google, which Epic won. Internationally, Google reached a settlement with Canada in November 2023, agreeing to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) annually for news content use, "with funds distributed based on the news outlets' headcount," establishing a precedent for publisher compensation that informed the Helena World Chronicle complaint's demands for consent-based AI training data usage.

# Default search engine placement as scarce asset in Google antitrust litigation

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google centers on deals making Google the default search engine across devices and browsers. A default search engine is the query service preselected by a device or browser maker so users search through it without setup action. This placement itself constitutes the scarce asset that Google and competitors vie for, as evidenced by Google's $26.3 billion spend in 2021 to secure default status across platforms including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. Internal Google data from 2007 showed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they performed "15% more Google searches," establishing early recognition that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share."


---


# Google's $26.3 billion 2021 default search payments

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Prabhakar Raghavan, Google's search head, testified on 28 October 2023 that Google had paid "$26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms" including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla to secure default search engine placement. # Google–Apple search deal: mutual obligations blocking competition since 2003

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that under a Google–Apple agreement dating to 2003, Google pays Apple (approximately $18 billion annually as of 2021) to make Google the default search engine. In exchange, "Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users," according to Bloomberg reporting cited in the article. This restriction prevents Apple from switching to a Google competitor or offering users browser choice during iPhone setup.
